prompt: You must choose a synthesis approach for a first instrument on a small microcontroller with limited RAM. You want classic analogue-style basses and leads and you want to learn each building block. Which choice best fits, and why?

options.text: Sample-based, because playback is the cheapest CPU operation
options.explanation: Sample playback may be efficient, but a substantial recording library needs storage and does not directly teach waveform generation. Filters can still be learned in a sample-based instrument.

options.text: Additive with 200 partials per voice, because it can make any sound
options.explanation: A large additive bank offers detailed spectral control but requires many component evaluations and controls. It is an unnecessarily demanding starting point for the stated sounds and learning goals.

options.text: Subtractive, because a few simple blocks give the target sounds and each block can be built and tested alone
options.explanation: Correct. A band-limited oscillator, a resonant low-pass, two envelopes and an LFO produce classic basses and leads, fit in small memory, and decompose into testable exercises.

options.text: Physical modelling, because it has the lowest memory use of any method
options.explanation: Some physical models are compact, but this does not establish a universal memory ranking. A subtractive voice more directly matches the stated learning goals; physical models can also be used creatively beyond acoustic imitation.

workedExample: A subtractive voice directly matches the requested bass and lead sounds, with oscillator, filter and envelope blocks that can be tested separately. A large additive bank increases per-voice work; a recording library may increase storage. These are implementation trade-offs, so measure the chosen design rather than treating the method name as a CPU or memory guarantee.
